talks.title: A New HOPE Begins!
talks.teaser: Welcomes attendees to the 2022 conference with its history, house rules, program overview and volunteer calls.
talks.summary:
The opening session of A New HOPE, the 2022 hacker conference held at St. John's University in Queens, New York, looks back at the event's history. The organizers recall the first HOPE in 1994 at Hotel Pennsylvania, explain that a steep price increase at that hotel pushed them to find a new venue, and note that the 2020 edition went virtual because of the pandemic.

Much of the session covers practical rules. Masks are requested except when on stage, eating or drinking; the venue is non-smoking and dry; and the code of conduct centers on treating one another well. Attendees can reach volunteers in green, security in blue, or campus public safety for issues. The session also walks through the schedule: more than 70 talks across three tracks, workshops on hardware and radio topics, DJ sets and live performances, capture the flag, and a coffee house open mic. Simulcast rooms link to the sister event May Contain Hackers in the Netherlands, and the Matrix chat and Mozilla Hubs serve virtual attendees.

The session closes with Wi-Fi details, the wiki, and calls for volunteers at the info desk and volunteer site. Organizers thank the volunteers and ask attendees to stay hydrated and look out for one another, framing the weekend as the start of the event's future.

talks.title: Secrets of Social Media PsyOps
talks.teaser: Traces the history of psychological operations and shows how targeted ads and bot networks are used to sway voters.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a definition of psychological operations, meaning non-combat efforts to shape the beliefs and behavior of an opponent or a population. It then walks through historical examples, including ancient intimidation tactics, wartime leaflet drops, and radio broadcasts during the Vietnam and Gulf wars. Throughout these examples, the speaker argues that propaganda works by targeting fatigue and basic emotions such as fear, greed and pride.

The middle section shifts to social media, where ads can be targeted by likes, searches and social connections instead of reaching a broad audience. The speaker covers the Cambridge Analytica case, in which a personality quiz collected data that was used to build psychological profiles for political ads. The talk then describes Russian-linked fake accounts, fabricated news sites and bot networks that amplified divisive content on both sides of political debates. A hypothetical campaign built around a fictional claim shows how a persuasion operation is planned, from choosing targets to distributing content and evaluating results.

The talk closes with practical defenses: use ad blockers, avoid quizzes that collect personal details, check who wrote a story and where it came from, and compare coverage across several outlets. The audience Q&A returned to fact-checking, the difficulty of changing someone's mind, and why people accept false stories that match their existing views.

talks.title: ActivityPub Four Years Later: The Good, the Bad, and the Fedi
talks.teaser: Looks at how the ActivityPub federated standard has fared since 2018 and why it remains a niche alternative.
talks.summary:
Rolltime, a long-time user rather than a spec author, revisits ActivityPub four years after it became a W3C standard. The talk starts by explaining federation: independent servers that pass messages on behalf of their users, sitting between fully centralized platforms and peer-to-peer designs that break when nodes go offline. It then traces the early fragmentation of federated systems, where incompatible protocols kept users apart, and how a single standard emerged to unify them.

The middle section looks at Mastodon as the largest platform in the fediverse. It covers chronological feeds without an algorithm, local and federated timelines, instance-level rules and blocking, content warnings, and alt text tooling. The speaker also points to gaps: the spec has no built-in identity or consent mechanism, implementations diverge on features such as follow requests so actions do not always reconcile, and most platforms are close clones of one another.

The closing argument is that adoption has stalled because timelines serve a consumption model shaped by corporate incentives. The speaker urges listeners to join the network, help improve the spec, and build interactive, creation-oriented social features instead of copies of existing products. Audience questions covered self-hosting, mobile push notifications, cross-posting bridges, and whether the protocol can succeed without mainstream adoption.

talks.title: Why Building Digital Libraries Matters
talks.teaser: Explains why digital libraries matter and how a large-scale book digitization pipeline works behind the scenes.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by asking what a library is, settling on an accessible, organized collection of materials with real value, and then asks who builds them, from national libraries to private firms. The speaker draws on about five years spent building the platform that digitizes books at the Internet Archive.

The pipeline runs from camera-based scanning stations spread across several sites, through upload and automated preprocessing, to a human review stage where operators check and correct the results before derived formats such as PDF, EPUB and text are generated. The hardest problems were mostly operational: catching errors quickly, keeping the service usable for scanning staff during outages, handling network failures with retries and caching, and dealing with physical logistics and unreliable consumer hardware and drivers. Human operators stay in the loop because books vary enormously in format and condition, so automation mainly reduced cost rather than improving quality.

The second half argues that digital copies matter because availability drives preservation, and that features such as full-text search, deep links into citations and embedded media add value beyond print. Free access is presented as essential to equality and trust, with digital originals serving as a lender of last resort. The talk closes by encouraging listeners to use, support and contribute to digital libraries.

talks.title: Six Years Later & Worse Than Ever - The Espionage Act, Computer Fraud & Abuse Act
talks.teaser: Examines how the Espionage Act and Computer Fraud and Abuse Act are being used against whistleblowers and journalists.
talks.summary:
This panel looks at the Espionage Act of 1917, a wartime law originally aimed at interference with foreign relations and neutrality, and at how it is now the main tool for prosecuting government whistleblowers. The speakers explain that its central provision can reach employees, members of the public, journalists and non-citizens alike, and that it is strict liability, so a person's motive offers no defense.

The discussion traces how prosecutions grew from the cases opened in 2010 under the Obama administration to a sharper escalation under the Trump Justice Department, including the indictment of Julian Assange and longer sentences for defendants such as Daniel Hale. Pretrial secrecy, limits on what defendants can say about their motives, and reported mistreatment of detainees are presented as serious concerns. The panel argues that these cases threaten national security journalism and anyone who publishes information in the public interest.

The second half covers legislative efforts that started after the Assange indictment, including a bill introduced in 2020 that would require proof of specific intent, allow a public interest defense, test whether information was properly classified, let defendants explain their purpose, and narrow who can be charged. The speakers describe slow progress, coalition building with newer lawmakers, and the difficulty of winning support. The takeaway is that reform will likely take years, and that engaging lawmakers and protecting sources matters now.

talks.title: Porn Platforms Hate Them for Exposing Their Mischief With These Two Weird Tricks
talks.teaser: Shows how a nonprofit audits a major adult platform's recommendations and third-party trackers with free tools.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how the nonprofit Tracking Exposed audits the recommendation system of a major adult platform. The speakers created test accounts across gender identities and sexual interests, then compared what each one was shown. Graphs of the overlap revealed two clusters: a heteronormative group and a less heteronormative one that was harder to map to channels.

The middle section covers the tooling. Potrex is a browser extension for collecting recommendation data. Guardoni is a Node-based tool that launches a clean Chromium profile from a JSON list of steps, captures screenshots, and records cookies, local storage and third-party trackers. The team argued that the trackers operating around adult sites have received little scrutiny from regulators or researchers.

The legal portion argued that online adult content sits in a legal vacuum, with gaps in laws, platform policies and norms around gender expression. It reviewed GDPR and its privacy-by-design principle, earlier EU rules on cookies and intermediaries, and the incoming Digital Services Act. The talk ended with policy, advocacy and litigation as possible routes, and a Q&A where the audience debated whether recommender bias is a technical or social problem. The practical takeaway is a repeatable method for auditing opaque recommenders with controlled accounts and clean browser profiles.

talks.title: All About RADIO WONDERLAND
talks.teaser: Explains how Radio Wonderland remixes live commercial radio into funk performances using custom Max code and everyday objects.

talks.title: Moving Beyond Amazon Self-Publishing Purgatory
talks.teaser: Discusses moving past being stuck in Amazon's self-publishing ecosystem.

talks.title: The CFAA Has Come a Long Way, or Has It?
talks.teaser: A panel of prosecutors, agents and a lawyer weighs what the 2022 Justice Department guidance changes for security researchers.
talks.summary:
This panel examines the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, the decades-old federal hacking statute, and why its central phrases, unauthorized access and exceeding authorized access, were never defined in the text. The speakers, a federal prosecutor, an FBI cyber agent and a former FBI supervisor who is now a lawyer, explain how Supreme Court rulings have narrowed the law and how Justice Department guidelines issued in May now direct prosecutors to decline cases involving good-faith security research carried out to avoid harm.

The middle of the session focuses on what the guidance does and does not change. The prosecutor stresses that the guidelines are internal policy that cannot be enforced in court and do not alter the statute, while the agents say their caseload is dominated by ransomware and other serious intrusions. The panelists then work through two hypotheticals: an incident response team that uses stolen cloud storage credentials to reach its data and deletes other victims' files, and a researcher who rushes out a patch for a wormable flaw. They weigh criminal exposure, civil liability and the risk of unintended damage, especially in hospitals and other systems that are hard to patch.

The takeaway is that the guidance signals priorities rather than rewriting the law, so teams should bring in law enforcement before acting on stolen data and document their intent and the care they took. Audience questions raised whether Congress should add a public-interest defense and how the Aaron Swartz case would be treated today, and the panel offered no firm answer on either. Responsible disclosure remains a matter of ethics and practice rather than statute.

talks.title: Open Source RF Experimentation
talks.teaser: Surveys open source software-defined radio hardware and software projects, from cheap receivers to amateur radio firmware.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with an overview of software-defined radio, a design approach where most signal processing happens in software rather than fixed analog circuits. The speakers compare low-cost receive-only dongles with transmit-capable devices and explain why an inexpensive receiver is a sensible place to start experimenting.

The middle section walks through specific open projects. These include the M17 digital voice mode, a budget amateur radio transceiver kit whose oscillators and filters are controlled by a microcontroller, and the HasViolet LoRa project built on Raspberry Pi Zero hardware. The HasViolet link was tested across a river at very low transmit power. The speakers also described a fox-hunting transmitter concept, SDR Angel as a multi-mode application, the SigPi package-based distribution for Raspberry Pi, and OpenRTX, which replaces firmware on existing handheld radios.

The closing remarks stressed that hardware and software are increasingly blended in open projects, and that experimenters should stay within licensed or permitted spectrum and avoid interfering with others. The session ended with audience questions about satellite communications, emergency amateur radio support and cellular network experimentation.

talks.title: Nikola Tesla's Predictions Today
talks.teaser: Panelists from the Tesla Science Center revisit Nikola Tesla's forecasts and update attendees on the Wardenclyffe project.
talks.summary:
The session opened with staff from the Tesla Science Center at Wardenclyffe, the site of Nikola Tesla's laboratory on Long Island. The organization explained its goal of encouraging people to question assumptions and treat inquiry as a habit. Fundraising was reviewed, with roughly eleven million dollars raised toward a twenty million dollar capital campaign. A recorded message from the executive director described the past year, including strategic planning, delayed permits, expanded tours, and youth coding and STEM programming.

The middle of the talk moved to Tesla's forecasts. Speakers discussed his predictions about pocket communication devices, wireless information networks, and wireless power, and compared them with what has and has not happened. A remote-controlled boat he demonstrated in 1898 was presented as an early ancestor of radio control and drones, and the panel argued his radio work was underrecognized. They also addressed his mistakes, including his support for eugenics and forecasts that never materialized. Current projects, such as a Tesla valve applied in a robotic heart research project and a large portable Tesla coil used to study lightning, showed that some of his ideas are still being tested.

The session closed with audience questions about which researchers continue this work. The panel pointed attendees to the organization's booth and community programs. The main point was that Tesla's unfinished ideas remain open problems for hobbyists and researchers to test, rebuild, and question.

talks.title: Hacking Local Politics: How We Banned Facial Recognition in Minneapolis
talks.teaser: Explains how a Minneapolis coalition used municipal politics to pass a ban on government facial recognition.
talks.summary:
The speakers, one from the ACLU of Minnesota policy team and one a freelance technologist active in a Restore the Fourth chapter, describe how the Safety Not Surveillance coalition pushed Minneapolis to restrict government use of facial recognition. The effort began in 2020 around a council data privacy resolution. After public attention shifted to police reform that year, the group narrowed a broader surveillance bill into a facial recognition ban. The council passed it unanimously, and the mayor let it stand without a signature.

The middle of the talk covers how local government really works. Each city has its own charter and structure, and much of the substantive drafting happens informally with staff, city attorneys and clerks. Power mapping, an old organizing method, charts council members and groups by influence and support. Lobbying is framed as persuasion: getting meetings, keeping messaging consistent and maintaining relationships. Coalitions are described as fragile, and technologists are encouraged to contribute practical skills such as websites and basic IT support while others handle community outreach.

The speakers acknowledge the limits of this approach. A single city has limited reach while data sharing continues at county, state and fusion center levels, and law enforcement opposition and low lawmaker awareness persist. They suggest scaling local wins upward, joining national networks such as the Electronic Frontier Alliance, and working with partners you disagree with on a single policy. They close with a power mapping walkthrough, showing how to find council members and their campaign pages, and urge newcomers to start small and stay persistent.

talks.title: How to Run a Top-10 Website, Publicly and Transparently
talks.teaser: Shows how Wikipedia runs a top-ten site in public, with open monitoring, public logs and volunteer access to help fix problems.
talks.summary:
This talk examines how Wikipedia, one of the most visited websites, is run by a non-profit with its operations kept largely in public view. It opens with the project's collaborative history and talk pages, then tours the infrastructure: code hosted on public review systems, metrics on open dashboards, documentation on wikis, and weekly deployments that volunteers can review and approve.

The middle covers how openness works in practice. Production configuration is published, and anyone can rebuild a near-identical environment in virtual machines, while redacted database replicas let people run SQL queries from a web tool. A late-2021 upload slowdown serves as a case study: the investigation happened in a public ticket, and a volunteer with no server access noticed that HTTP/2 was causing far more round trips between data centers than HTTP/1.1, which led to the fix. Public IRC channels and an archived server admin log record changes and outages.

The talk is also candid about the costs. Private logs and server access require signing an NDA, and volunteer root access has become harder to obtain as operations teams professionalized. Keeping work public is an ongoing fight, since teams drift toward closed chat tools and permanent archives can follow contributors for years. For smaller sites, the advice is to start gradually: document components, publish configuration, and track bugs openly. Security through obscurity is rejected in favor of staying current on patches.

talks.title: Keynote and Q&A
talks.teaser: A former Facebook data scientist describes how governments used fake pages to manipulate their own citizens.
talks.summary:
Sophie Zhang, a former Facebook data scientist, joins interviewer Yan Zhu for a discussion and audience Q&A. She describes her role on a small team that hunted fake and inauthentic activity in her spare time, and how checking who liked a politician's post revealed networks of pages run by governments. Those networks used loosely verified pages, rather than fake user accounts, to flood political debate with praise for leaders and attacks on opponents.

The conversation turns to why the work went unaddressed. Zhang points to reactive handling driven by outside pressure, teams judged on numeric metrics, and policy decisions entangled with political relationships. She argues that spotting deception from outside is very hard without internal data, and suggests trusted red-team style testing as a way to measure how platforms perform. She also warns that a flood of convincing fake content could erode trust online more broadly.

Zhang explains the care she took to gather evidence, the difficulty of choosing a reporter, and the legal and personal costs she has faced since going public. She admits that her memo was written in haste and that she would seek support, such as legal and PR help, earlier. The session closes with questions from the audience.

talks.title: Leaks and Hacks: Four Years of DDoSecrets
talks.teaser: Explains how the DDoSecrets collective collects, publishes and vets leaked datasets, and the ethical trade-offs involved.
talks.summary:
The speakers from DDoSecrets, a transparency collective founded in 2018, review the group's first four years of publishing leaked and hacked data. They trace its path from early Russian and government datasets to large releases such as BlueLeaks, the Parler archive, ransomware leak-site scrapes and, more recently, material linked to the war in Ukraine. Most of the archive is public, while sensitive sets go only to vetted researchers and journalists under limited distribution. A search index helps people find which dataset holds a given keyword.

The middle of the talk focuses on the practical difficulty of working with huge, unstructured leaks. Newsrooms often lack the staff or training to go through terabytes of files, and records can depend on local language, slang and institutional knowledge that a small volunteer group cannot supply. One example is a police-related dataset that arrived as a web application database, spreadsheets and PDFs, which had to be reconstructed before reporters could use it. The presenters also cover ethical questions around personal information, armed conflict and state-linked sources, and explain why they avoid giving any single outlet exclusive access.

In the questions, the speakers discuss how the group decides whether material is in the public interest, how outside researchers can request limited-distribution access, and how they manage safety and legal threats through redundancy and shared responsibility. The takeaway for practitioners is that large leak archives only become useful when someone invests in verifying and contextualizing them, and that publication choices shape both risk and impact.

talks.title: Mad as Hell: Is There an End to Subversion?
talks.teaser: Examines whether pranks, stunts and context hacking can still produce subversion in a media landscape built on spectacle and control.
talks.summary:
Johannes Grenzfurthner, an artist, filmmaker and member of the Monochrome collective, opens by asking what subversion can still achieve when little shocks anyone anymore. He frames his practice as "context hacking," the idea that where and how a message is placed decides whether people hear it. He traces this back to hacker pranking at MIT and to his own youth in Austria, where a fanzine and bulletin board were attempts to reach people beyond underground circles.

The middle of the talk moves through personal stories, including his grandmother's reaction to E.T. and his parents' new-age beliefs, which he tested with a pendulum experiment. He contrasts the older disciplinary society, where hierarchies made rebellion easy to spot, with a society of control in which people police themselves through friendly bosses, reassuring cameras and gamified labor. He also argues that nerd culture now holds real power, and that conspiracy thinking grows from a search for meaning and scapegoats.

He closes by warning that slogans such as freedom are easily co-opted, and that meaningful change comes from many small actions in daily life rather than from a few prominent figures. He admits he has no tidy answers, leaving the audience with questions about how to reach people who disagree.

talks.title: Online Operations for Protests and Pranks: How to Get the Truth Out
talks.teaser: Shows how online protest pranks drew press coverage and stayed live under takedown complaints from registrars and providers.
talks.summary:
The talk examines online protest and satire aimed at large corporations, drawing on climate activism linked to Extinction Rebellion and the tactics of the Yes Men. The speakers start with a fake announcement attributed to Google about its funding of climate-denial lobbying groups. Mainstream outlets picked it up, and the presenters explain how spreading it through activist networks, alongside a self-hosted site, helped it travel. They connect the result to the Streisand effect and to a "decision dilemma," where any response from the target feeds the campaign.

The middle section covers two more actions. A meme challenge aimed at cloud providers' fossil fuel contracts drew little press because it was spread over three weeks, which the speakers present as a lesson in timing and narrow targeting. The largest case was a fake community outreach campaign run by the owner of a Wisconsin refinery, using mailed postcards and press releases. It drew local coverage and, by their estimate, reached several hundred thousand people or more. The infrastructure lessons come from the takedown complaints it triggered: use several domains and registrars, shorten every link, avoid large registrars, respond quickly to complaints, and be careful about collecting email addresses, which led to phishing accusations. Email accounts were also banned, so they recommend keeping backup addresses.

The closing argues that stunts alone do not change policy and that sustained movement pressure does. The Q&A covers corporate responses, whether share prices move, and alternative email providers.

talks.title: Demand Protest: Manufacturing Truth in a Post-Truth Era
talks.teaser: Traces how a fabricated company gained media credibility, showing how online hoaxes spread and how they can be countered.
talks.summary:
The talk traces how online hoaxes have grown from chain emails and folklore into tools used by governments, companies and activists. The speaker starts with legend tripping, the real-world pursuit of supernatural stories, then moves through transmedia storytelling, from an early bulletin-board mystery to commercial alternate reality games. Further examples include a fabricated 2014 chemical plant explosion tied to a Russian influence contractor, a polished propaganda channel linked to a religious movement, and the Georgia Guidestones, where a long-running conspiracy story ended with the monument being blown up.

The centerpiece is Demand Protest, a fake company the speaker built to appear to run paid protests. The hoax combined a detailed website, job postings, a phone line and fake operative logins, and was seeded in fringe forums until mainstream outlets reported it. The goal was to have the media debunk a story it had amplified. When a prime-time cable host confronted the speaker on air, the hoax was exposed, though some outlets kept repeating the claims afterward.

The practical takeaways are to read sources across the political divide, to challenge unsourced claims publicly, and to support accessible public news. The speaker also recommends pre-bunking, building trust before manufactured doubt arrives, and cautions that censorship can push people into more extreme networks. Audience questions covered how real paid-crowd firms operate and how individuals can check original sources.

talks.title: Hackers Got Talent
talks.teaser: Hackers present their own talents and hacks onstage, judged by a panel and the audience for a prize.

talks.title: ARTificial Intelligence - How IP Law Handles Machine Creations
talks.teaser: Explains whether machine-generated output can qualify for patent inventorship or copyright under current intellectual property law.
talks.summary:
The talk starts by defining the systems in question: large machine learning models, usually deep neural networks, trained on big datasets. The speaker treats such a network as a function that maps inputs to outputs, and argues that the real difference from ordinary software lies in how it is built. He then points to generative examples such as DALL-E images and Google's LaMDA writing a short fable as the outputs that raise intellectual property questions.

The main question is whether those outputs can earn copyright or patent protection. For copyright, protection requires human authorship and a modicum of creativity, and bare ideas are not protected. He reviews Stephen Thaler's cases, including a rejected copyright filing for a creativity machine and a patent application naming an AI as inventor that has reached the Federal Circuit. For patents, inventorship depends on conception, which he finds hard to attribute to a machine, and he compares unfiltered model output to the infinite monkey thought experiment.

He concludes that DALL-E output is probably not copyrightable and that the person writing the prompt would not own it, though a human who curates or arranges outputs creatively may have a stronger claim. He flags open issues such as whether training on copyrighted material is fair use. Questions from the audience covered standing, drug discovery, and code generation licensing. The takeaway is that the law remains unsettled and human contribution is the factor to watch.

talks.title: Using Security Automation to Organize Your Cyber Threat Intelligence Knowledge
talks.teaser: Explains how security automation can help organize cyber threat intelligence knowledge.

talks.title: Electronic Warfare on a Budget of $15 or Less
talks.teaser: Explains radio fundamentals, electronic warfare tactics, and low-cost software-defined radio for listening to everyday signals.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the physics behind radio: any wire carrying an oscillating current radiates, so nearly every everyday device is a transmitter. Wavelength tied to frequency sets the antenna length needed, and improvised field antennas cut from coax show how this works in practice. The spectrum is then sorted by band, with lower frequencies penetrating better and higher ones carrying more data.

Next comes electronic warfare, split into protection, attack and support. Encryption, jamming, directional jamming against key links, direction finding by triangulation and rapid frequency hopping are each weighed against the countermeasures they invite. Transmitters can also be fingerprinted from the startup transients of their oscillators, which reflect manufacturing tolerances. Rarer channels such as meteor burst links, skywave HF, over-horizon radar, very low frequency submarine signaling and number stations round out the section.

The second half focuses on cheap software-defined radio, which handles demodulation in software and covers a wide band for very little money. Demonstrations include plotting aircraft ADS-B broadcasts, listening to pilot messages, mapping ship AIS traffic, decoding pagers, and detecting hydrogen-line radio astronomy signals. The speaker stresses that transmitting needs filters and checks against local regulations. The closing takeaway is that the hardware barrier has collapsed, but care still matters.

talks.title: How to Bargain With a Black Box: Hacking a Path to Data-Driven Organizing
talks.teaser: Shows how simple data tools helped platform workers challenge an opaque algorithmic pay change and support organizing.
talks.summary:
Dan Calacci, a PhD student at MIT, argues that the labor movement needs people with technical skills to build tools for workers. He opens with a retailer's delivery platform that moved drivers from a transparent per-order percentage to a black-box pay algorithm in 2020. Drivers began sharing pay screenshots online, and the pattern suggested that many were earning less for similar orders.

An organizer collected these screenshots, and the team built a simple texting bot that read them with OCR and logged pay details into a shared spreadsheet. About 200 workers signed up within two weeks. The analysis showed that a large group had taken pay cuts, which supported a report and further protests. The talk then covers related projects: a phone app that gathers sensor data stored privately on the worker's device, spreadsheet templates for reconstructing unpaid hours, and digital workshops with unions in the Global South. A worker-led campaign also used the app to document unsafe late-night commutes.

Dan describes the obstacles, including employer wearables that collect data workers cannot access, often treated as trade secrets. He points to California's AB 701, which lets third parties request warehouse quota data on workers' behalf, and to data trusts and cooperatives as collective governance models. He closes with a 1913 long-exposure photograph of workers' motion, urging designers to keep people visible in data systems. The takeaways: work alongside worker groups, build tools that workers can adapt, and keep control of data with the workers who produce it.

talks.title: Revolution During Disintegration: A Brief History of Yugoslav Computing
talks.teaser: Traces how Yugoslavia's in-between Cold War position shaped its mainframes, home computers and packet networks.
talks.summary:
Vlado Vince presents a history of computing in Yugoslavia, a socialist state that was not aligned with the Soviet Union and traded with the West without joining NATO. He argues that this in-between position shaped what its engineers could build, buy and connect, and he draws parallels to today's tech sanctions and export controls.

The enterprise thread follows Digital Equipment Corporation, whose partnership with Yugoslav engineers grew into Iskra Delta, a firm that built PDP-11 compatibles under license. The home-computing thread centres on Galaksija, a magazine-driven do-it-yourself microcomputer whose designers published schematics and parts lists so readers could import components and assemble machines, which thousands did before import rules loosened. The networking thread covers the JUGPAK packet network, built separately by each republic, and the scramble to reach the internet as the country broke apart. Late-1980s bulletin board systems linked people across republic lines, and an anti-war BBS network later relayed messages into besieged Sarajevo.

The closing lessons are that import limits tend to be worked around, that hacker and open-source habits appear under constraint wherever they are, and that keeping communication open during war has real humanitarian value. Vince also cautions against judging people by their country, and the session ends with questions about his sources, which are mostly local-language materials.

talks.title: Five Dollar Cyber Weapons and How to Use Them
talks.teaser: Surveys cheap microcontrollers that run Wi-Fi attacks, BadUSB payloads and beginner CircuitPython projects.
talks.summary:
Kody Kinzie opens by framing the talk as an introduction to offensive work on low-cost microcontrollers, many of which now cost less than five dollars. He contrasts them with single-board computers like the Raspberry Pi, whose prices have climbed, and explains the skills needed for each route: flashing community firmware through a browser, copying CircuitPython onto a board as a USB drive, or compiling Arduino code for finer control.

The middle of the talk moves through specific boards and projects. The ATtiny85 and ATmega32u4 cover keystroke injection and mouse jiggling, with a warning that the cheapest boards are unreliable across different computers. The Raspberry Pi Pico runs Ducky-style scripts. The ESP8266 is the centrepiece because older firmware allows raw Wi-Fi packet injection, which powers the Deauther project. Demonstrations include deauthentication, rogue access points, a phishing page posing as a router update, probing for networks stored on phones, spoofing assisted GPS locations, signal-strength presence detection, drone-based searching of a park, and NAT routing. The ESP32 adds packet capture, and the ESP32-S2 brings native USB and CircuitPython, although newer Espressif chips restrict packet injection.

The closing section covers the USB Nugget and a deliberately vulnerable web login app for practising with proxy tools, then previews newer boards such as the ESP32-C5 and C6. The takeaway is that meaningful attacks are within reach for a few dollars and that formal computer science training is not required to start, though hardware quality can vary between suppliers.

talks.title: Seize the Means of Computation: How Interoperability Can Take the Internet Back
talks.teaser: Argues that interoperability can lower switching costs and push Big Tech to treat users better.
talks.summary:
Cory Doctorow argues that Big Tech should be weakened rather than tamed, and that technology should be run by and for the people who use it. He traces how dominant platforms took hold after US antitrust shifted to a consumer welfare standard that stopped treating monopoly itself as harmful. The key concept is switching costs, the price of leaving a service, such as losing contacts or uploaded photos. When those costs are high, people stay even when they are badly treated, so lowering them forces companies to compete.

The middle of the talk defines interoperability, from formal standards to reverse engineering. Doctorow cites Apple's iWork suite, which reverse engineered Microsoft Office file formats to keep documents compatible, and a Massachusetts automotive right-to-repair mandate that carmakers sidestepped by moving diagnostics to wireless links. He contrasts rigid legal mandates with flexible but chaotic adversarial interoperability, and argues that combining them is stronger. Obstacles include anti-circumvention and computer fraud laws, and platforms' use of moderation and security arguments to block rivals.

He closes with practical levers: legal defenses for interoperability work, procurement contracts that bar vendors from attacking interoperators, funding for maintainers of public-interest code, and public campaigns that explain what is being lost. The audience Q&A covered content moderation, privacy law with private rights of action, and emulation for digital preservation.

talks.title: Closing Ceremonies
talks.teaser: Wraps up the weekend's event with a look back at how it went and its memorable moments.

talks.title: Engineering Your Own Disease Eradication Program
talks.teaser: Shows open-source tools for automated chemical synthesis, a DIY defibrillator build, and home-made emergency medicine kits.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with an audience Q&A in which attendees suggest illnesses and medicines the Four Thieves Vinegar Collective should prioritize next. The speaker explains that the group does not invent new science. Instead it revives established technologies that were neglected, left unpursued, or priced out of reach, and makes them buildable by individuals.

The main segments cover an updated MicroLab, a small automated chemical reactor built from off-the-shelf parts with no soldering required. A new Recipe Press tool generates run files through pull-down menus, including prompts that ask a human operator to check progress. A web-based planner then searches chemical literature and proposes synthesis routes for a small molecule, with filters for precursor availability, and the speaker runs it live. Next comes an open-source automated external defibrillator, adapted from an earlier design in a master's thesis, with parts costing about six hundred dollars. Its capacitor charging, biphasic output and rhythm-analysis logic are explained. Simpler add-ons for cardiac arrest, such as an oxygen blast and epinephrine auto-injectors, follow. Reproductive health kits are presented last.

The talk closes with calls for volunteers and donations, with the speaker saying logistics costs more than the drugs. The main takeaway is that managing one's own health is presented as a right, and that audience priorities should shape what the group builds next.

talks.title: The Mathematical Mesh
talks.teaser: Presents an open infrastructure for managing private keys so encrypted data works across a user's devices and colleagues.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the regular stream of data breaches and asks why personal data is not simply encrypted. The speaker argues that encryption is the easy part. The hard part is getting encrypted data onto every device a person uses, sharing it with colleagues, including those who join later, and recovering it after a loss. He presents the Mathematical Mesh as an open specification with reference code that handles private key management, so that applications do not each have to solve it.

The demonstrations cover a sequence of scenarios. A second laptop is joined to an account by sending a connection request, comparing a short verification value on both sides, and granting only the privileges the device needs. Key generation is split between the two devices, so the final key stays secure unless both fail. Group decryption is shown next: a file encrypted to a group becomes readable to a newly added member and stops being readable when that member is removed. Service providers hold key shares that let them withdraw decryption ability without being able to decrypt anything. Contact assertions and trust tracking are presented as ways to keep a relationship stable when messaging providers or addresses change. A browser built on WebView2 shows access to one website being granted and revoked.

The closing section sets out a wider goal: open alternatives for messaging, bookmarks, social media and internet-connected devices that users own rather than rent from a vendor. The speaker asks for contributors and notes that anyone can run a service provider with a static address and a domain name. The code is published on GitHub under an MIT license. The main takeaway is that threshold cryptography can spread control of keys across several parties instead of concentrating trust in one.

talks.title: In Which Interlaced Video Digitization Makes Me Forget About Dying (For a While)
talks.teaser: Follows an archivist digitizing decaying VHS tapes, covering the workflow, tooling choices and why preserving everyday media matters.
talks.summary:
Archivist Jason Scott, who works with the Internet Archive, opens by explaining how he takes on at-risk media that others have no plan to save. A pile of VHS tapes, including fan-subtitled anime recordings from a closed New Jersey shop, set him on a long digitization project. He describes the basics of standard-definition interlaced video and the mechanical fragility of the tape decks that read it.

He then walks through his workflow: a capture card, open-source capture software, and a lossless codec that consumes huge amounts of storage, with several decks running at once. Before settling on this method he surveyed hobbyist digitizers online and collected their tool choices and frustrations. The middle of the talk moves to a collection bought at auction from a deceased musician's estate, which held recordings of New York club scenes, early computing promotions, interviews and local broadcasts. Scott also describes the personal toll of losing colleagues and family, and how steady archival work helped him cope.

He closes by urging listeners to record what matters to the people around them, including conversations with relatives, and to keep a practical, non-destructive process going rather than waiting for ideal conditions. He also shares a brief note on the deinterlacing filters he uses.

talks.title: Plausible Deniability and Cryptocurrency Privacy
talks.teaser: Panelists explain how blockchain users can avoid leaking identifying metadata when transacting in Bitcoin, Ethereum and privacy coins.
talks.summary:
The panel opens by challenging the belief that Bitcoin, Ethereum and similar networks are private by default. Transactions on public chains are visible to anyone, and the speakers stress that pseudonymity is not anonymity. They cite cases where people were identified through on-chain activity, and they define plausible deniability through the idea of an anonymity set, where a participant cannot be singled out from at least k others.

The middle section maps where users leak identifying data. Public RPC endpoints see the IP address of the sender, block explorers log visitors, and exchanges that hold identity records can be subpoenaed. Reusing addresses links activity together, and account-based chains such as Ethereum expose more by default than UTXO chains. Timing habits and manually chosen gas prices can also fingerprint a user. Mixers that pool fixed denominations can break those links, but withdrawing too soon or on a predictable schedule shrinks the anonymity set. Zero-knowledge proofs and trusted execution environments are described as approaches to private verification, each with cost and trust tradeoffs.

The closing discussion turns to usability and policy. The panelists argue that wallets and apps rarely ship privacy by default because users do not demand it, and that people using privacy tools openly helps keep them from being marked as suspicious. They say most privacy losses come from user error and encourage practitioners to learn the tools and push product teams toward better defaults.

talks.title: Travel Hacking in a Still-Pandemic World
talks.teaser: Covers the practice of travel hacking in a world still shaped by the pandemic.

talks.title: Tracking Android Malware and Auditing App Privacy for Fun and Non-Profit
talks.teaser: Walks through static and dynamic analysis of Android apps to audit privacy leaks and dissect malware behavior.
talks.summary:
Bill Budington, a technologist at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, opens by explaining that a popular Play Store app and a piece of sideloaded malware can be examined with the same toolkit. He describes how APK files are structured and where Android apps are distributed, including alternative marketplaces and their risks, and introduces apkeep, EFF's command-line tool for batch downloading apps.

The middle of the talk covers static analysis with jadx, which approximates the original Java, and apktool, which produces smali that can be modified and rebuilt. Frida handles runtime instrumentation, while mitmproxy and certificate bypasses expose encrypted traffic. Two case studies follow: a privacy audit of the Ring doorbell app, which sent data to several third parties, and a Tor-based trojan that posed as a banking app, abused accessibility permissions, and loaded hidden payloads. Obfuscated strings in that payload led to an onion service that revealed a clearnet command-and-control login page.

The talk closes with a field setup that places the proxy, Frida and SSH on one rooted Android device running Debian, so a remote auditor can monitor traffic outside a lab. The takeaway is that apps may behave differently when they know they are being watched or when they depend on location, so monitoring on the device itself can reveal their real behavior.

talks.title: Quantum Computing: It's Not Just Sci-Fi Anymore
talks.teaser: Explains quantum computing basics, post-quantum cryptography risks, and how to try quantum systems through free cloud tools.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by saying he is not a quantum expert and wants to point the developers in the room toward quantum tools they can use now. He contrasts classical bits with qubits, using the Schrödinger's cat thought experiment to explain superposition, and notes that quantum machines are built for specific problems such as factoring, protein folding, and optimization rather than general-purpose computing.

He then covers the hardware at a high level: quantum processors are kept close to absolute zero using superfluid cooling, and superconducting qubits are controlled with microwave pulses. The security focus is Shor's algorithm, which threatens RSA and elliptic curve cryptography, while symmetric encryption is expected to hold up better. He points to NIST's selection of post-quantum algorithms such as CRYSTALS-Kyber and Dilithium, and argues that encrypted data captured today could be decrypted later, which makes migration urgent.

The talk closes with access options. Cloud services from AWS, Azure and IBM let people rent time on real quantum hardware for small per-job fees, and free simulators are available. He walks through a short two-qubit example in IBM's open-source Python SDK, then lists community resources such as the Unitary Fund, quantum training lists and a quantum computing subreddit for anyone who wants to get involved.

talks.title: void loop () - Minecraft as My Musical Instrument
talks.teaser: Shows how Minecraft becomes a live musical instrument, using Ableton Live audio routing and Twitch chat commands to drive performances.
talks.summary:
Ramon Castillo, an associate teaching professor of music at UMass Lowell, explains how he turned the game Minecraft into a performance instrument. The work began in 2020, when the pandemic moved his ensemble online and real-time playing was lost. He wanted live interaction with an audience, and he saw that the game's redstone, command blocks and mods could be manipulated to produce sound.

The middle of the talk covers the technical flow. Game audio is routed through Ableton Live, where effects and envelope following are applied, and MIDI signals drive character movement through a Teensy board acting as a human interface device. A Twitch chat bridge, built with Max for Live and Node.js, lets viewers issue commands such as turning the character. He demonstrated a 24/7 installation with a jukebox, a solfeggio piece, a maze whose audio changes as the player moves, and a university server with student projects built on mods such as Create. Video from the game is also color-keyed and processed in VDMX.

He closed by performing excerpts from the void loop pieces and noting limits in the setup, including that ClyphX Pro is no longer maintained, and he invited collaborators to add tracks or ideas. The practical takeaway is that game sounds can be replaced and processed like a sampler, and that chat-driven control of a live game is achievable with off-the-shelf music software and a small microcontroller.

talks.title: From Mind Control to Mind Expansion: Hacking Technology to Rebuild Our World
talks.teaser: Reframes society as a system hackers could rethink, and explores using VR, brain-computer interfaces and AI in unintended ways.
talks.summary:
The session opens by arguing that the world feels like a system in crisis, and that hackers, who are used to finding flaws in technical systems, should also look at the larger system that governs society. The speakers use three metaphors to frame this: machines, networks and games. They argue that machine-age thinking, with centralized controls and rigid authority, keeps pulling networks back into fixed structures. They also warn about optimizing for a single score, illustrated by a reinforcement learning agent that looped in a boat racing game to maximize its points instead of finishing the race.

The middle of the talk compares possible approaches to change. Building entirely new virtual worlds from scratch is unrealistic, and simply augmenting existing structures tends to get absorbed by them. The speakers favor an extended reality approach that builds new possibilities alongside existing systems, interoperating with them on the builders' own terms. They walk through examples: digital goods that replicate for free, ride-sharing as proof that information flows can reorganize physical transport, the role of artificial scarcity and abundant funding in shaping what gets built, and how crowdfunding and patronage could be made more direct. A drug-synthesis collective was cited as a concrete case of applying open tooling to a hard-to-access resource.

The talk closes with an invitation for attendees to locate their own position relative to the system and to start small, building proofs of concept that others can follow. In the question period, the speakers recommended work on adversarial interoperability and the book Finite and Infinite Games, and offered a follow-up workshop for interested attendees.

talks.title: Hack the Planet... Step 1, Step 2, Step
talks.teaser: Explains what penetration testing means in practice, how CREST accreditation works, and what buyers should expect from providers.
talks.summary:
The session opens with CREST, an accreditation body that has been assessing penetration testing providers since 2006, explaining why the term is so loosely understood. Because buyers use terms like vulnerability assessment, ethical hacking and red teaming interchangeably, CREST published an approved penetration test specification that sets minimum expectations for scoping, delivery and sign-off. The speakers stress that the goal is commercial defensibility, and they describe tiers of individual competence, from practitioner through registered to certified, as a way for buyers to judge who they are hiring.

A penetration testing provider then walks through a healthcare client's cloud assurance engagement. The scope was black box and adversarial, so the team started from public infrastructure and mobile apps. A decompiled Android app led to an endpoint whose stack trace exposed a bearer token for a Microsoft Graph API with broad permissions. Validating the token showed access to user lists, files and the ability to send mail as other users. Because this was production, the team informed the client at once, and testing paused while the client remediated. The walkthrough tied each stage to a repeatable process: kickoff, reconnaissance, testing, exploitation, reporting, debriefs and cleanup.

The question-and-answer session covered reporting for non-technical executives, with an executive summary framed in business risk and separate technical detail. Speakers noted that CREST is not a pass or fail audit. Applicants that fall short are coached and can resubmit, individuals are reassessed every three years and organizations yearly. The practical takeaway for buyers is to state clearly whether they want a CREST-accredited test, define their goals and scope up front, and expect consistent, usable reporting.

talks.title: Right to Repair - You Should Have the Right to Fix What You Own
talks.teaser: Traces how a repair video channel grew into a legal campaign for owners' right to fix their own devices.
talks.summary:
Louis Rossman opens by showing how small failures, such as a dead motor in a medical table or a faulty charging chip in a laptop, become expensive because manufacturers restrict parts, schematics and service access. He explains that his repair business started almost by accident, and that he later realized how hard it was to buy legitimate parts compared with earlier decades, when manuals and components were widely available.

The middle of the talk covers the arguments he has faced at legislative hearings. He recounts claims that repairs cause explosions, fraud or physical danger, and a safety-themed advertising campaign used against a bill in Massachusetts. He argues these claims fall apart under scrutiny and points to an FTC report that examined manufacturer claims. He describes how a donor-funded advocacy organization shifted the effort from individual repair toward broader control over owned technology, including locked bootloaders, software subscriptions and DMCA section 1201 restrictions. Audience questions covered New York's law, tractors, warranty voiding and how to start learning board-level repair.

He closes by urging advocates to frame repair around people's self-interest, to build skills through small early wins, and to support repairable alternatives such as certain laptops. The takeaway is that repairability is both a policy fight and a skills problem that technically capable people can help solve.

talks.title: Breaking 19th Century Encrypted Newspaper Ads With Modern Means
talks.teaser: Traces 19th century encrypted newspaper ads through their history and shows how classic ciphers can be broken with free tools.
talks.summary:
Elonka Dunin and A.J. Jacobs present a collection of encrypted classified advertisements printed in English, French and American newspapers during the 1800s. Their co-author Klaus Schmeh could not attend, so the two presenters covered the material between them. Newspapers were read in port cities around the world, which made printed notices a practical way to pass messages, and many notices were enciphered to keep their contents private.

The talk moves through several case studies. The best known is a run of ads from the 1850s linked to a search for the Franklin expedition in the Arctic. That cipher was eventually solved by spotting common words, such as the name of a month or the word for sun, and matching them against a code book from the period. Other examples include romantic exchanges broken with frequency analysis, a message from 1873 cracked with software that tests letter patterns against English words, and a 1902 ad that was only solved in 2014 after its alternating letters were split into two sequences. A single Denver ad that remains unsolved is also covered, along with ciphers from the Enola Holmes film and the coded notices of private detective Ignatius Paliki.

The presenters close by inviting the audience to help with the messages still open. They point to free software and online services as practical starting points. The main takeaway is that substitution and code-book methods, combined with historical context and open tools, can still reveal old messages, and that many others remain open puzzles.

talks.title: Unpickable But Still Unlockable: Lock Bypass Tricks in the Field
talks.teaser: Shows which physical lock bypass techniques hold up in real field tests and which fail under time pressure.
talks.summary:
The session starts from the goals a physical red team works toward: imitate a real intruder, keep each bypass defensible if someone walks up, move quickly, and stay quiet. Before attempting anything, the presenters map every possible entry path, weighing time, camera coverage and sensor triggers, and test the worst case for the defender. They then walk through common non-destructive methods, including latch poking with cards or slip tools, under-the-door handle tools, and pulling loose multi-bank doors, noting that dead latches defeat several of them.

Field results were mixed. Wheelchair push buttons sometimes unlock locked doors, fire-code egress doors release during alarms, and an alarm panel can be reset with a screwdriver. Propped or warped doors, false ceilings and vents offered easy routes. A purchased magnetic alarm lock could be defeated by placing a surrogate magnet. Hinge pin removal and keypad box tricks such as factory default codes or fob cloning were noisy, slow or hard to undo, so they were judged limited in practice. Socially, calm body language and a plausible role such as maintenance or a supervisor often got the team past staff.

The main takeaways for defenders are to segment space so tailgating into inner areas is less valuable, to tune request-to-exit sensors, to test alarm response times, which were sometimes 45 minutes or more, and to build a security culture where staff question unfamiliar visitors. Bringing facility contacts on engagements was presented as more effective than carrying an authorization letter alone. Cameras were described as unreliable under changing light and weather, so the response process matters as much as the hardware.

talks.title: Executive Order 14028 & Zero Trust Architecture - Now We Must, But What It Means?
talks.teaser: Explains what Zero Trust means under Executive Order 14028 and why identity management sits at its core.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at Executive Order 14028, issued in May 2021, and the federal strategy that followed in January 2022 to move US government agencies toward Zero Trust Architecture. The speaker argues that the term is overused and misunderstood, and that vendors often sell it as a product. He recalls asking booth staff at a major security conference what they meant by Zero Trust and getting mostly inconsistent answers. He frames it as a long journey and a change in mindset rather than a checkbox.

The middle section traces the idea from early work by the Jericho Forum and the BeyondCorp model to NIST SP 800-207. The speaker argues that cloud services, remote work and personal devices have made network-based trust obsolete, so every request should be verified against context, with privileges granted narrowly and removed afterward. Identity becomes the foundation, covering users, devices, services and data. He warns that tokens can be copied or replayed and need their own protections, and that usability and privacy must be designed in rather than traded away. Open standards and interoperability are presented as part of the answer, with one open-source identity project offered as an example of building blocks, while the speaker notes it does not solve every problem.

In the closing question round, the discussion turned to legacy industrial control systems that cannot be replaced quickly. The speaker suggested stopgaps such as reverse proxies and microsegmentation. The practical takeaway is to identify your crown jewels and weakest points, prioritize the highest-impact steps, and expect the model to keep evolving.

talks.title: How Hip-Hop Can Inspire the Next Generation of Tech Innovation
talks.teaser: Explores how hip-hop music and culture spur innovation across science, education, health, politics and journalism.

talks.title: Project MKULTRA Cracked: Declassified CIA Brain Warfare Research
talks.teaser: Shows how public records and academic acknowledgments were used to rebuild the identities behind CIA MKUltra sub-projects.
talks.summary:
The talk separates the popular myth of MKUltra, with its Manchurian candidates and trauma-based mind control, from what the CIA program actually involved. The speakers describe it as a research and development effort from 1953 to 1964 that funded 149 sub-projects through front organizations at 86 North American institutions. Some financial records survived the 1970s document destruction, and the presenters start from congressional reviews and earlier indexes compiled by John Marks and Colin Ross.

The method combines several kinds of open-source material. Job titles left unredacted in CIA documents can be searched to identify researchers. Grant records from a CIA-funded society for the investigation of human ecology match dollar amounts in the agency files. Acknowledgments in academic papers then tie specific published research back to those funders. Examples include a language-teaching machine project linked to Harvard and a project on synthesizing LSD. Together these steps produced a cracked index that identifies roughly 80 percent of sub-projects, which the speakers compare against the earlier books' indexes. An artwork visualization displays the results.

The takeaway is that the surviving documents show a body of drug and behavior research carried out through academic cover, rather than a single programmed-assassin project. Questions afterward covered sloppy redactions, modern FOIA responses, and cooperation with Canada and the UK. The speakers note that the remaining gaps are largely classified or unverified.

talks.title: Proof of Vaccination Technology and Standards
talks.teaser: Explains how proof of vaccination credentials use signed QR codes and public keys to resist forgery while minimizing disclosed data.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the case for digital proof of vaccination credentials, needed once businesses, venues and governments began asking people to show they were immunized. The speaker frames the goals as revealing only what a verifier needs, working across jurisdictions, and letting holders present the credential without any remote database lookup.

The core design pairs a human-readable page with a machine-readable QR code that carries a compact signed payload, following the SMART Health Card format used in Canada and many US providers. The payload holds a name, birth date, vaccine details and validity. The issuer's public key is published at a known web location instead of being embedded, because a forger could otherwise slip in their own key. Verifier apps cache issuer keys and per-jurisdiction policy files so they can check signatures offline. A live demonstration showed a genuine code passing and an altered one failing. Revocation lists cover compromised keys or bad vaccine lots, and the talk noted the lack of federal coordination in the US compared with Canada's shared issuer list.

The closing argument was that blockchain was unnecessary: signed documents, public key cryptography, minimal data and cached trust lists met the requirements, including offline use. The main risks sit in a few well-protected points, such as issuer lists and signing keys. Questions covered key rotation, certificate expiry, malicious issuers and extending the standard to other vaccines.

talks.title: Hacker Representation Through the Years: Hacker Appearances in TV and Cinema
talks.teaser: Traces how hackers have been portrayed on television and in film across the decades.

talks.title: Demoscene: Electric Boogaloo
talks.teaser: Traces the demoscene from BBS-era cracking and copy parties to modern shader showdowns and tiny executable art.
talks.summary:
This talk walks through the demoscene, a computer art subculture that pushes machines to their limits to produce graphics, music and code. It opens with early networking history, including the first shared games between schools, then moves through modem-era bulletin boards, commercial online services and file sharing. Cracking groups' intros and disk magazines eventually gave rise to European copy parties, where piracy gave way to competitive art.

The middle section follows the shift from simple intros to cinematic demos in the early 1990s, with examples from the Amiga and PC scenes. The presenter then covers size categories such as 64-kilobyte and 4-kilobyte productions, programs only a few hundred bytes long, and demos written for unusual hardware, including game consoles, handhelds and vintage home computers. Live coding contests, such as shader showdowns and size-limited competitions, are shown as current trends, along with executable graphics, where a complete image is rendered by a tiny program.

The closing segment points to the scene's modern events, both in person and online, and suggests ways to find demos and parties. The main takeaway is that the scene rewards creative constraint, and that people with programming, art or music skills can take part without a formal background.

talks.title: Social Steganography: Sending Messages in the Clear for Fun and Nonprofit
talks.teaser: Shows how selective truths and ambiguous wording can shape messages in public, using state wiretap and recording laws as examples.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the idea that persuasion works through what is left out as much as what is said, and that a message posted openly can be read very differently by different audiences. The speaker introduces social steganography as writing that is understood by readers who share context while others miss its meaning, and argues that many people wrongly assume public speech is safe from misreading or legal consequence.

The middle section goes through practical rhetorical habits: staying deliberately ambiguous, telling selective truths, being specific when addressing a particular audience, and escalating quickly with facts when someone misreads on purpose. These are tied to legal questions, including two-party consent recording laws in several US states, truth as a defense against libel, and how a Pennsylvania constitutional clause and a computer-crime statute might apply to scraping and good-faith security testing. The speaker also covers how weaknesses in carrier signaling (SS7) and older mobile encryption make phone calls less private than people assume, and why routing Tor through a VPN can undermine anonymity.

The talk ends with an open question-and-answer session. The speaker notes that some techniques were left out of the presentation, and invites further discussion of censorship circumvention, encryption and privacy. The practical takeaway is to assume a message may reach audiences the author did not intend, and to check the legal context of recording and system access before acting.

talks.title: Shoplifting on a Budget: Exploring Bypasses for Retail Security Tags
talks.teaser: Explains how retail anti-theft tags work and demonstrates physical methods for getting past several common types.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who presents under the handle MakeItHackin, traces the idea back to a viral short video about foil-wrapped tags and a physics lesson on Faraday cages. The talk then lays out how retail electronic article surveillance works: gates at the store exit, detachers at the checkout, and tags built on three technology families that operate at different frequencies. Most tags rely on friction or a magnet to stay locked, which is why a magnet is the usual way they are released.

The middle of the session walks through hard tags, ink tags, soft labels, spider wraps and security boxes, and notes which ones are deactivated at the register and which stay on the item. The speaker demonstrates a range of physical approaches, including cutting conductive traces, separating locking pins with improvised levers, containing ink with tape or glue, and shielding RF tags in foil-lined bags. Several methods were tested on camera, and audience volunteers tried a spider wrap and a foil bag on stage, with mixed results.

The closing portion covers the legal side, stressing that shoplifting is illegal and that carrying a tool into a store to defeat a tag can bring an extra charge. For loss prevention teams and decision makers, the takeaway is that tag style matters: hook-style tags were described as harder to open and less responsive to magnets than other designs. The speaker then answers audience questions about accidental alarms and airport security.

talks.title: Quiet! How Local-First Software Can Keep Remote Teams Safe and More
talks.teaser: Shows how a Tor-based, peer-to-peer team chat app syncs data without a cloud server, and how that approach could extend to other tools.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the argument that cloud dependence has weakened free software's ability to hold large tech companies accountable. When data and relationships live on company servers, the freedoms to run, study, change and redistribute code offer little practical leverage. The speaker points to Reddit's move away from releasing its code as an example, and describes servers as creating censorship, lock-in, volunteer burden and competitive problems.

The middle of the talk is a live demo of Quiet, a team chat app in which members' devices connect directly to each other over Tor onion services. Invitations work through an onboarding service on the owner's device, and state is synced with a conflict-free replicated data type over an IPFS-based gossip layer. The demo covered message sync, sharing a large file and inviting a new user. Performance tests showed average delivery under two seconds at modest message rates, with a delivery spike in a 100-user test. Known gaps include no mobile push notifications without a server, timed deletion not yet implemented, a single owner who must be online to issue invites, and no security audit yet.

The closing section compares Quiet with related projects such as Briar, Cabal, Pinecone and Secure Scuttlebutt, and surveys the local-first software movement. The speaker's main request is for small groups with real privacy needs to trial the tool and report back, and for developers to contribute to the effort.

talks.title: Remember the Internet: Hacking Publishing
talks.teaser: Shows how a small press runs a no-overhead publishing model while chronicling internet history one book at a time.
talks.summary:
The speakers, who run Instar Books, open by breaking down what a publisher actually does. They describe five core jobs: production, editorial work, marketing, publicity and operations. Their argument is that these jobs, rather than any special gatekeeping quality, define the value a publisher adds between writer and reader, and that the relationship works more like a partnership than a judgment.

They then explain their own approach. The company handles production in-house, sells ebooks directly to keep a steady income, contracts out publicity, pays small advances with royalties, and compensates the founders largely in equity rather than cash. It started with no money and funded its first titles from its own books. They say it has stayed profitable, though the model depends on the founders holding other jobs, which limits how many titles they can produce.

The centerpiece is the Remember the Internet series, short templated books that each examine a discrete online moment, such as Tumblr porn, a Tori Amos bootleg webring and Google Glass. The series grew out of an opt-in project that collected message board posts from a dying user, and the speakers discuss balancing personal memory with journalistic history. They also cover digital experiments, plans for a second season, and an audience discussion about what counts as the internet. The takeaway for practitioners is that a small team can publish niche work sustainably if it plans each title carefully and owns distribution.

talks.title: Hacking the SAT
talks.teaser: Shows how multiple-choice tests like the SAT can be answered by test-taking shortcuts that bypass understanding the content.
talks.summary:
Rob Cohen, a former math teacher who now runs a test preparation business, argues that multiple-choice standardized exams have predictable weaknesses that can be exploited. He starts by stating his disapproval of these tests and recalls a tutoring session in which he realized a student could reach the correct answer without understanding the underlying concept.

He then walks through several techniques. Past exams are public, and some state laws require releasing questions, so studying the most frequently tested categories is an efficient starting point. Other approaches include spotting grammar rules such as dangling modifiers, reading linear equations in word problems, plugging simple numbers into abstract algebra, and using a graphing calculator, whose supplemental software the test does not restrict. He also covers answer elimination, guessing patterns, and the advantages extended-time accommodations can give, which he considers unfair to students without them.

He closes with the shift toward test-optional, test-flexible and test-blind admissions, and the College Board's plan to move the SAT to a digital format. He is skeptical that a redesign will make the test harder to game. The main takeaway is that many multiple-choice questions can be answered without mastering the material, which matters for anyone who relies on those scores.

talks.title: Hacking the Anthropocene: Life, Biological Complexity, Freedom!
talks.teaser: Explores how biological hacks like modularity and reuse generate complexity, and how those ideas apply to social systems.
talks.summary:
The talk reframes hacking beyond its old-school engineering sense, asking whether the ecological and social crisis of the modern era can be approached as a computational problem. The speakers begin by asking what life is, using two lenses: assembly theory, which treats the number of construction steps a molecule needs as a possible sign of life, and autopoiesis, which describes a living system as a network of relationships that reproduces itself.

They then treat evolution as a process of accumulating complexity while exploring a space of possibilities. Examples include the beak shapes of Darwin's finches, the new territory that opened up when birds evolved powered flight, and biological hacks such as multicellularity, the modular genetic code, genome plasticity and whole-genome duplication, which they compare to forking a software project. Losing lineages, giving up sexual recombination and ecosystem tipping points are presented as forms of lost information. Collapse is compared with Joseph Tainter's account of diminishing returns on complexity, and the rise of photosynthesis is described as a phase transition rather than a simple catastrophe.

In the final part, freedom is framed as agency, which depends on information, time and space together. The speakers argue that hacker communities are strong on information but need more capacity in the other two areas, and they offer a three-part lens for judging projects. In the question period, a listener linked immune system pruning and neural development to a cycle of expanding and reducing complexity, and the speakers agreed that complexity is a tool rather than an end goal. The practical takeaway is to assess efforts by how well they combine all three dimensions over time.

talks.title: We'll Pwn You With Your Wattpad Profile
talks.teaser: Explains how leaked password hashes get cracked and how a GPT-3 model guesses passwords from profile data.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the attacker's side of a data breach. Leaked databases often hold password hashes rather than plaintext, but a cracker can run large lists of candidate guesses through the same algorithm offline and compare the results against the leak. The speaker walks through how this works, moving from brute force to dictionary wordlists, combined words, common character substitutions, and phrase-based tricks that turn a memorable sentence into a short string of initial letters.

The middle of the talk covers a student research project. The team fine-tuned GPT-3 on about 10,000 examples drawn from a 2018 Wattpad breach, pairing profile fields such as usernames and bios with the passwords tied to them. Given a target's public details, the model produced guesses that outperformed a list of common passwords within a small number of attempts, and the speaker reported roughly three times the accuracy of non-targeted guessing. The work was small and the speaker described its limits openly. The question round covered entropy thresholds, comparison with other targeted guessing tools, and the ethics of the study.

The closing section turns to defense. Long, unique passwords, password managers such as Bitwarden or KeePassXC, and Diceware-style passphrases for critical accounts reduce exposure. The speaker suggests estimating entropy against a realistic threat model, so that memorable passphrases still hold up against guessing.

talks.title: You'll Pay For That: Payment Systems, Surveillance, and Dissent
talks.teaser: Traces how payment systems and cryptocurrency rules are used for government financial surveillance and what that means for dissent.
talks.summary:
Alex Marthews, who leads the civil liberties group Restore the Fourth, opens with a personal example: his children could not ride fairground rides in China because the only accepted payment, WeChat Pay, requires a Chinese national ID. From there the talk traces how financial surveillance grew, starting with anti-terrorism financing rules after 2001, the Holy Land Foundation prosecution, and the pressure on WikiLeaks and crowdfunding platforms to cut off donations.

The middle section covers the expanding reach of the US government into cryptocurrency. Marthews describes transaction reporting thresholds, prosecutions of peer-to-peer traders, and contracts with blockchain analytics firms that can cluster addresses and follow change outputs. He discusses a recent executive order on digital assets and the possible move toward central bank digital currencies. He then gives examples of activists, students and charities in Venezuela, Afghanistan, Iran, Nigeria and Belarus using crypto to keep funding their work outside the banking system, and explains why privacy coins have not yet been used at scale to blunt sanctions.
