The closing part looks ahead: discouraging cash, merging credit rating agencies with data brokers, and corporate payment platforms that could be aligned with government demands. His suggestions include choosing smaller credit unions, splitting digital identity into separate claims for separate contexts, and trying an unhosted privacy coin wallet to understand the trade-offs. Audience questions covered delisting of privacy coins, illicit finance concerns, and whether blockchain identity can be made safe.

talks.title: Why Professor Garfield Should Be Your Child's Best Friend on the Internet
talks.teaser: Makes the case for a familiar cartoon cat as a guide to children's safety on the internet.

talks.title: CHERI: A Modern Capability Architecture
talks.teaser: Explains how CHERI adds hardware capabilities to processors to enforce fine-grained memory protection without relying on secrets.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the argument that memory safety bugs such as buffer overflows and use-after-free still account for most serious software vulnerabilities, decades after the problem was first widely understood. Using a short C program on a RISC-V target, the speaker shows how a processor that treats pointers as plain addresses cannot notice an out-of-bounds write, so corruption spreads silently until the program fails far from the original bug.

The core of the talk explains CHERI, an extension to existing instruction sets that turns pointers into hardware capabilities carrying an address, bounds, and permissions. Memory keeps a hidden validity tag for each 16-byte granule, and any operation that tampers with a capability clears its tag, so the processor traps instead of silently corrupting state. The speaker covers how compilers, the loader, and the kernel adapt, how ported software such as FreeBSD and much of KDE needed little change, and how sealed capabilities support compartmentalization and cheap communication within one address space. Temporal safety is addressed with quarantine and revocation sweeps, and performance results from the research hardware are reported.

In closing, the speaker argues that capabilities complement safe languages such as Rust, since a sandbox around unsafe code can turn hardware traps into recoverable errors for the safe side. Arm's Morello prototype shows the design running on real silicon, though it is an experimental platform rather than a product. The Q&A covered speculative execution, where capabilities reduce some attacks but do not stop side-channel leaks of ordinary data.

talks.title: Cyber Security Certifications: The Good, The Bad, and The Ugly
talks.teaser: Sorts security certifications by real career value, from entry-level credentials to senior ones, and flags the ones to avoid.
talks.summary:
Tom Kranz, drawing on about thirty years in IT and security, argues that certifications are widely misunderstood by candidates and employers alike. He starts with the history of security credentials, pointing out that the field still lacks a settled definition of its roles, which makes certifications attractive but easy to misread. He criticises popular certification maps and the simple analyst, engineer and architect career model as a poor fit for how people actually work.

The middle of the talk sorts certifications by quality. Credentials he considers worth pursuing include CompTIA Network+ and Security+ for entry level, Cisco's CCNA, ISACA's CISM, the OSCP for hands-on offensive work, and the CISSP for experienced practitioners, provided the candidate already has the years of experience it assumes. He warns against pay-to-play courses, tool-focused training, vendor-specific credentials that can pigeonhole people, and promises of automatic salary increases. He also covers SABSA, TOGAF, SANS GIAC, the free EU-backed Concordia C3 course, university degrees, and CREST, including the reported exam-cheating controversy and its effect on trust in the scheme.

He closes by urging listeners to treat certification as proof of skills they already have rather than a shortcut into a job. Practical exams and continuing education make a credential meaningful, while a certification that never expires says little about current ability. He points to a separate interview workshop for more detailed career advice.

talks.title: hCaptcha: Profits over People and Fscking Useless
talks.teaser: Examines how hCaptcha's accessible workflow raises privacy concerns and can be automated, and what should replace puzzle CAPTCHAs.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with assistive technology and how CAPTCHAs are meant to separate people from automation, then focuses on hCaptcha, a commercial provider used by a large share of websites. The speaker walks through the standard visual challenge and the accessible alternative, which takes several steps: requesting access by email, clicking a link to set a cookie, and sometimes contacting support for manual approval. The accessible path is noticeably longer than the visual one.

The speaker raises two problems. The first is privacy: because the accessible cookie is tied to the email address used to sign up, it could in principle be linked to a person across sites. The second is security: the accessible flow contains no step that verifies a human, and a scripted browser with a custom mail handler was able to complete the entire process. Rate limits were the only visible countermeasure. The vendor disputed earlier research and said the attempt was likely caught, and both the vendor and Cloudflare declined to treat the report as a security issue through their bug bounty programs.

The talk then looks ahead. hCaptcha is testing a text-based challenge that the speaker expects to be more accessible and privacy-friendly, though it is still in beta. The speaker argues that puzzle CAPTCHAs are losing value and points to hardware-backed and zero-interaction attestation as better options. The takeaway is to design for all users from the start, since separate accessible workflows tend to be slower and less private.

talks.title: Botnets are the Best Way to Measure User-Hostile Behavior on the Internet
talks.teaser: Explains how volunteer-run measurement botnets can study dark patterns and other user-hostile web behavior better than bot farms.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a research problem: web measurement studies need to observe how sites treat visitors, including dark patterns such as hard-to-find cancellation flows and misleading consent dialogs. The speaker reviews the two usual approaches. Bot farms are fleets of automated browsers run on servers the researcher controls. They are costly to maintain, behave in ways that sites can detect, and offer little network diversity. Piggybacking uses browser extensions installed by volunteers, which adds a privacy and performance burden for participants and limits measurements to whatever sites those people happen to visit.

The middle of the talk presents an alternative: a measurement botnet in which a small client runs on volunteers' home machines, pulls studies when spare capacity is available, and returns compressed, signed results. The client isolates the browser on Linux using systemd sandboxing with system call filtering, namespaces and control groups, and it claims only a fraction of system resources. Volunteers can schedule ride-alongs to watch what the bot is doing, and studies can ask a human for judgments on pages, which helps with subtle design choices that are hard to model automatically. The speaker also explains the choice of a fork of OpenWPM for browser instrumentation and covers design questions such as Docker versus native isolation and macOS support.

The closing part addresses risks and open problems: poisoning by untrustworthy participants, which may be countered by re-measuring the same sites, and legal uncertainty under computer misuse law and terms of service. The talk ends by placing measurement botnets within a history of volunteer distributed computing and invites contributions on isolation, scheduling, bot detection, packaging and incentives.

talks.title: Creating a General Purpose Network Through Wireless Mesh
talks.teaser: Shows how a city-wide mesh network independent of the internet can carry offline archives, radio data and emergency communications.
talks.summary:
Jameson Dungan describes a wireless mesh network he is building in Norfolk, Virginia, meant as a general-purpose network that runs independently of the internet and could keep working during outages or emergencies. He walks through the hardware, including directional links between buildings, access points, outdoor-rated cabling, cheap used antennas mounted on rooftops, and solar and battery backup. He also explains the basics of the first three OSI layers and how the network is routed.

Software-defined radios and small Raspberry Pi nodes collect local data such as aircraft and ship broadcasts, NOAA weather satellite imagery and accurate time from a GPS-based server. Offline archives, including Wikipedia, Project Gutenberg, Stack Overflow and medical references, are hosted on the network. The talk then turns to amateur radio, covering packet systems that can relay messages and reach SMS and email, along with routing protocols such as OSPF and Babel that suit mesh topologies.

The closing section covers the non-technical side: getting access to rooftops and buildings, partnering with local groups and the city, and inviting others to add nodes and content. Dungan stresses learning by iterating and sharing failed tests. The Q&A raised open problems such as delay-tolerant networking and distributed naming. The network is still early and mostly a one-person effort.

talks.title: Designing for Privacy in an Increasingly Public World
talks.teaser: Shows how dark patterns and data sharing erode user privacy and how designers can build transparent, privacy-first experiences.
talks.summary:
Robert Stribley, a digital designer with two decades in the field, argues that designers should treat privacy as part of the experience they build. He frames privacy as control over personal information and explains why the stakes have grown, pointing to data breaches, identity theft, facial recognition built from publicly posted photos, and tracking of health-related browsing that became more sensitive after abortion rights changed in the United States.

The middle of the talk covers dark patterns, interface tricks that steer people into choices they did not intend. Examples include a pre-selected recurring donation, opt-out buttons that shame the user, and contact-importing prompts that send invitations to a person's friends. He reviews apps and services that made activity public or intrusive by default, and compares the EU's GDPR, which requires opt-in consent, with the American opt-out approach. He also notes that a few ordinary data points can identify someone even without obvious identifiers.

The closing section offers practical guidance: make privacy the default, avoid dark patterns, explain data use in plain language at the moment of collection, place privacy controls where people can find them, and warn users before changing their settings. He also suggests that designers push back on clients by framing privacy as a matter of reputation, legal exposure and cost. The takeaway is that privacy by design is a practice teams can adopt now, not only a legal requirement.

talks.title: Let's Talk: Bioprinting
talks.teaser: Offers a conversational look at bioprinting, the 3D printing of biological materials.

talks.title: Novel Exploitation Tactics in Linux Userspace One Byte OOB Write to ROP Chain
talks.teaser: Shows how a one-byte out-of-bounds write can grow into a full ROP chain under seccomp without any leaks.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from "houses," reusable exploitation patterns that turn heap bugs into code execution through glibc internals. The speaker argues that the runtime loader, rtld, has been less explored than malloc or stdio. Looking at the exit path, the speaker finds that thread destructors and exit handlers are protected by pointer mangling, so a weak bug cannot easily hijack them. Attention then moves to the dynamic loader's finalizer handling, which offers a different route.

Using that surface, the talk walks through a chain of techniques built for a CTF challenge. The target offered a single-byte out-of-bounds write, no output channel, no leak, a seccomp sandbox, and no brute force. The first step uses a link map field to keep the program looping, which turns the write into infinite writes. Next, a forged dynamic section lets the loader resolve and call arbitrary library functions without knowing the base address. A final construction uses the loader's symbol resolution to write chosen pointers to chosen locations, which is enough to assemble a ROP chain.

The main takeaway is that offsets are more useful than absolute addresses when no leak exists, because the loader works in relative terms. The Q&A made clear that statically linked binaries and full RELRO remove the lazy resolution this relies on, while partial RELRO leaves it exposed. The speaker pointed to a written write-up and slides for the detailed mechanics.

talks.title: Just Enough RFID Cloning to Be Dangerous
talks.teaser: Shows how cheap RFID access tags and hotel keys can be copied, with live demos using Proxmark 3 and common blockers.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a practical problem: the speaker needed to open a building garage while riding a motorcycle, and fishing a key out of a glove each time was awkward. It then explains how passive RFID works. A tag has no battery and powers itself from the reader's field, answering by modulating that field. Low-frequency tags are described as simple devices that return a fixed serial number, while high-frequency tags can run cryptographic routines and store data that a reader can update.

The middle section covers the practical side. It goes through common chip types, data formats and form factors, from cards and key fobs to rings and stickers, and the cheap cloners that handle simple cases. The main tool shown is the open-source Proxmark 3, which reads both frequency bands. A live demo reads a garage access badge and writes its data to a rewritable tag. A second demo reads a hotel key card, runs an attack against its encryption, and writes its unique identifier to a magic card. Several RFID blockers are also tested against both frequencies, including paper sleeves, fabric, pouches and an active card, with mixed results.

The talk closes by noting that copying these cards works only from very close range, and that high-frequency keys depend on their identifier and vendor-specific encryption. The practical takeaway is that simple low-frequency badges are easy to duplicate, while newer systems are harder to copy but not immune. The speaker points to hobbyist forums, vendor datasheets and explainer videos as places to learn more.

talks.title: Practical Steps to Improve Privacy
talks.teaser: Walks through free-software steps to reduce everyday passive surveillance across phones, computers, routers and messaging.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the premise that privacy is not the default and cannot be bought as a single product. The speaker limits the scope to passive surveillance, meaning what an individual can control on their own devices, rather than targeted attacks. He defines "free" as software you can run, study, modify and share, and proposes a "freedom ladder" that moves from store-bought devices toward fully free hardware and software. He argues that claims of security through obscurity and vendor promises cannot be checked without free software.

The middle of the talk goes rung by rung. It covers free Android builds such as LineageOS, GrapheneOS and Replicant, F-Droid as an app source, and freer desktop operating systems, along with alternative BIOS firmware such as coreboot and libreboot. It also covers routers that run OpenWrt or LibreCMC, offline password managers such as KeePassXC used with unique passwords, and browser hardening with Firefox-based builds, uBlock Origin, NoScript, LibreJS and Pi-hole for network-level blocking. Messaging is ranked by client, backend and federation, and self-hosting is presented as a way to avoid trusting third parties.

The closing portion and audience questions cover the limits of this approach: trusting VPN providers is hard to verify, smart TVs and car infotainment systems are difficult to avoid, and many newer phones still need proprietary drivers. The main takeaway is to make changes one at a time, favour software you can verify, and bring friends and family along by starting from their interests.

talks.title: An Engineer's Guide to Linux Kernel Upgrades
talks.teaser: Explains why Linux kernel updates are less risky than feared and how to schedule them safely in production.
talks.summary:
Many production teams delay Linux kernel upgrades because they treat the kernel as the most dangerous component to change. The talk argues that this fear is misplaced and that delay carries its own costs. Using data from the 5.15 stable branch, it shows that weekly bug-fix releases often contain dozens to hundreds of commits, and that most include at least one CVE fix. Waiting also widens the gap between the running and target versions, so breakage risk grows faster than the delay itself.

It then covers common anti-patterns: routing kernel changes through generic change-approval processes, asking whether each CVE is exploitable instead of patching, and soaking kernels for fixed periods rather than using measurable criteria. Kernel version numbers are not semantic versioning, so the leftmost number says little about risk. Bug-fix releases carry only fixes, while major releases bring features on a roughly nine-to-ten-week cycle. Live patching covers only a narrow set of cases because internal kernel data structures can change.

The takeaways are to apply bug-fix releases promptly, choose a long-term branch if validating each major version is too costly, and write acceptance tests covering the kernel features each workload depends on. Decisions should rest on metrics and test results rather than elapsed time. Automating rollouts also removes the hesitation individual engineers feel, and reboot-driven rollouts are naturally gradual, giving time to catch regressions.

talks.title: COVID Making: From Cyber Pantries to Cyber Glasses
talks.teaser: Shows how a volunteer built sensor alarms and ordering tools for a community food pantry, plus a wearable Raspberry Pi display.
talks.summary:
Matt Desmarais, who goes by Matt the Maker, describes the community food pantry he has volunteered with since 2007. The pantry ran on paper order forms, an old Access database and aging desktops, and it repeatedly lost food when freezers failed without anyone noticing. He begins with the pantry's distribution models, then explains how he tackled the freezer problem with low-cost sensors that log temperatures to a cloud dashboard and send text alerts when a door stays open or a unit warms past a threshold.

The middle of the talk covers the alarm logic he tuned by testing it on a deliberately unplugged freezer, the motion sensors that stopped false alarms during deliveries, and the separate rules he used for refrigerators. He then moved intake to Salesforce, Google Workspace, Formstack and Zapier during the drive-through period of the pandemic, and built a now-serving display and a packing-station feed. According to the order data he presents, letting clients choose their own items cut inventory use substantially.

The closing section turns to a wearable Raspberry Pi display he built in 2017 and rebuilt in 2021 with a camera, bone conduction audio and a gamepad-driven application launcher. His takeaway is that people with technical skills can improve local services, and that open-source hardware makes such projects affordable, while organizations still need simple, packaged solutions they can run themselves.

talks.title: Defensive Computing
talks.teaser: Shows non-technical users practical steps for DNS filtering, VPN checks, Chromebook guest mode, router choice and passwords.
talks.summary:
Michael Horowitz argues that tech press coverage of security tends to dwell on alarming disasters while offering little practical defense. He pitches the session at non-technical users, though he expects experienced people to find useful material too. He opens by criticizing how reporters cover privacy stories, then turns to email, noting that sender addresses are easy to forge and recommending a paid provider over a free one.

The middle of the talk centers on DNS. He explains the difference between legacy and encrypted DNS, shows that name resolution can be set by a router, the operating system or a browser, and demonstrates how a DNS provider can block ads, trackers and malicious domains. He compares several providers and points to Chromebooks as a strong default, with system-wide secure DNS and a guest mode that discards everything on exit. Other topics include router selection, outbound firewall rules, isolating devices on public Wi-Fi, and checking that a VPN really routes all traffic through its tunnel.

He closes with password advice, suggesting that the most important passwords stay out of password managers and that a fixed part plus a memorable variable part makes them easier to keep. He also recommends a sacrificial second phone number and warns that VPNs on iOS can leak traffic. The takeaway is to verify settings rather than trust defaults.

talks.title: How Do MRI Machines Work? An Introduction to MRI and Open Source Imaging
talks.teaser: Explains the physics and hardware behind MRI scanners, from magnets and RF coils to image reconstruction, with open-source imaging projects.
talks.summary:
Douglas Brantner, an MRI research engineer who works on motion sensors and test objects, gives a broad introduction to how magnetic resonance imaging machines function. He starts with the practical problems: patient motion degrades scans, metal and conductive parts are hazardous near the magnet, and scanners are expensive and hard to access. He also contrasts MRI with CT, noting that MRI uses no ionizing radiation, and surveys clinical uses such as functional imaging and contrast selection.

The middle of the talk walks through the physics. Hydrogen protons align with a strong static field and precess, and a radio frequency pulse tips them and brings them into phase. The resulting signal decays with T1 and T2 relaxation, and gradient coils shift the resonance frequency with position so the signal can be localized. Data is collected in k-space and converted to an image with an inverse Fourier transform. Brantner also covers superconducting magnets, cryogenic cooling, shim coils, and the Faraday cage around the scanner room.

Brantner then describes his own sensor work: testing non-magnetic components, measuring RF noise and field homogeneity with phantoms, and shielding a motor-driven motion phantom. He closes by presenting the Open Source Imaging project, which builds lower-cost and tabletop scanners and invites collaborators. The main takeaway is that MRI is a demanding, safety-critical engineering problem, and that open hardware efforts are trying to make it more accessible.

talks.title: Secure Cell Phone Communication: Mission Accomplished or Popular Delusion?
talks.teaser: Surveys phones built to resist data capture and assesses whether any secure option can compete with major carriers.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with an audience poll on how seriously people protect their communications, then argues that constant monitoring through a personal phone discourages people from speaking out and taking political action. The speaker frames the goal as a phone users can carry everywhere without feeling watched.

The middle section surveys the available options. Older handsets such as Nokia feature phones and BlackBerry devices were trusted for a time, partly because they ran little software and some had no microphone. Linux-based devices such as the PinePhone offer more control, including a modem that can be reflashed and a hardware switch to disable it, but they lack the mainstream apps people expect. Premium hardened phones with kill switches from several vendors were described as very expensive. The most promising candidate was a German vendor's Android-based phone with Google services removed, but the speaker found that US carriers could not supply instructions for using it on their networks and that the device had no US FCC license.

The closing takeaway is that no secure phone yet competes with the major carriers. The speaker suggests that a group of users buying these devices, sharing work on making them run on US networks, and creating demand is the most realistic path forward.

talks.title: The Ransomware Protection Full of Holes
talks.teaser: Shows how Windows 10 and 11 Controlled Folder Access can be bypassed through registry COM hijacking and folder relocation.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with Windows 10's built-in ransomware protection, added in late 2017 after WannaCry. Its core is Controlled Folder Access, which guards a list of protected folders and allows only approved apps to write to them. The speaker points out that many researchers have reported bypasses, and that Microsoft did not treat an earlier registry-based injection into File Explorer as a security vulnerability.

Prompted by a 2021 article that called the feature effective, the speaker retested the old injection on current Windows and found Microsoft had quietly fixed it on both Windows 10 and Windows 11. Searching further, the speaker found the default protected folders were defined under the current user's registry hive, so a user-level change could redirect them. Moving the Pictures folder left its original files outside the protected set, and those files could then be encrypted. A later demonstration combined a COM hijack with a remote network path, so an attacker who could write registry values could trigger encryption without delivering a payload to the target.

The takeaway is that these bypasses are simple, and the speaker stressed that they should not be used to build ransomware. Controlled Folder Access should not be treated as a complete barrier. Defenders should monitor registry writes to COM class keys and changes to known folder locations, and backups remain the most reliable protection against encryption.

talks.title: Beyond the Digital Nomad: Finding Refuge and Building a Life
talks.teaser: Explains realistic routes to work permits, residency and second citizenship, and how vulnerable people can find refuge abroad.
talks.summary:
Elior Sterling opens with a personal account: a childhood surrounded by Holocaust refugees, years of volunteering as a translator and with a cross-border aid group on the Tijuana and San Diego border, and a move abroad to escape a long stalking case. The talk is framed as practical life skills rather than legal advice, and the strategies are presented as relevant to people holding many different passports.

A large part of the talk covers deciding whether to leave and where to go. Sterling argues that a first destination is often a stepping stone, and that asylum systems frequently fail applicants with strong documentation. Routes presented include investor visas, points-based immigration systems, skilled-worker shortage lists, certifications treated as degree equivalents, remote work and internal company transfers, and ancestry-based citizenship. Marrying for a visa is discouraged. Disabled and trans migrants get dedicated sections on accessibility, healthcare continuity and support networks. For urgent cases, the talk describes living on tourist visa waivers while working remotely.

The closing questions covered tax obligations, which generally follow the employer's location or the passport country, the rules on giving up citizenship in some countries, and the added complexity of moving with children. The takeaways are to research visa rules early, network with people in the target country, visit before moving permanently, and keep a return ticket for the first trip.

talks.title: Combating "Ransom-War:" Landscape of Ransomware Infections in Cloud Databases
talks.teaser: Explains how ransomware and botnets infect cloud databases such as MongoDB and Elasticsearch, and demonstrates tools to detect them.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at ransomware and botnet infections that target databases behind modern cloud applications, with a focus on MongoDB and Elasticsearch. The speaker argues that attackers now go after the data itself, since controlling a database lets them demand payment or destroy the data so that applications lose availability. The attack paths covered include exposed administrative interfaces, weak or default passwords, unpatched database software, compromised endpoints that pivot into cloud environments, and phishing of cloud account holders.

The middle of the talk walks through real infected instances seen during the research. Ransom notes appeared as collection or index names, and in some cases indices were encrypted or renamed so the stored data became unusable. One case showed a ransomware group placing the name of a recovery firm into compromised data, which illustrates why threat intelligence needs careful artifact filtering. The speaker then demonstrates two open tools built to scan remote databases: basic checks that enumerate contents for ransom indicators, and intrusive checks that pull more detail from infected instances. Honeypot detection for Elasticsearch scanning is also covered.

The closing takeaway is that no single control is enough. Practitioners should keep database interfaces off the public internet, maintain hardening baselines and patching, run regular posture assessments rather than one-off tests, add anomaly detection alongside signatures, and watch outbound connections for signs of data exfiltration. Security checks before cloud database instances are deployed are recommended as a standing policy.

talks.title: Cat-Shaped Hacker Hardware: How I Accidentally Made a Business at 18
talks.teaser: Traces how a cat-shaped beginner hacking board grew from a spare-parts side project into a product, and the design missteps behind it.
talks.summary:
Alex Lynd recounts how a favor to a friend, selling leftover microcontrollers and screens, grew into a small hardware business built around the WiFi Nugget, a cat-shaped, Game Boy-style board for cybersecurity beginners. He starts with his own background in low-cost microcontrollers and signals intelligence, including a wardriving project and a commissioned device that tracked a lost phone by its probe requests.

The middle of the talk covers the design missteps. The first board was an all-in-one multi-tool meant to suit everyone, which left users unsure what it was for. The team then juggled several form factors, two microcontroller variants with overlapping names, and a software line that added to the confusion. Lynd contrasts this with a well-known security vendor whose devices each serve one clear use case. The cat theme eventually became the differentiator, and the team narrowed the product to a single board with a WiFi attack interface, followed by a USB attack package used for a soft launch of 300 units.

To close, Lynd distills a few lessons: pick one audience and one purpose, keep the product explainable in a single sentence, and build a brand around what sets it apart. He also describes a batch of 500 outsourced boards that arrived faulty because a swapped component was never tested, a reminder to validate every part before production.

talks.title: Don't Get Tangled up in Your Cape: Hero Culture as Negative Cyber Security Force
talks.teaser: Examines how hero culture fuels burnout, gatekeeping and toxic norms in security teams, and what organizations can change.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who has led security teams for many years, starts from a practical question: how do you build strong practitioners and teams when the field has so many open roles? He says the problem is not heroic action itself but a culture that makes heroic, round-the-clock effort the expected norm. He compares common superhero traits, such as unchecked action, limited accountability and being celebrated for saving the day, with how security work is often rewarded through bonuses, praise for weekend firefighting and crisis-driven recognition.

The middle of the talk covers the harm this culture causes. Staff who are cast as heroes often treat users and management as the villains, which encourages knowledge silos and a habit of holding onto control. Interview processes and internship postings that expect advanced skills can screen out newcomers and people who do not resemble the current team. The speaker also describes "brilliant jerks" who are protected despite damaging their colleagues, and how poor sleep, heavy drinking and burnout are treated as normal. He points to survey data on stress, turnover and staff shortages.

The talk closes with suggestions for practitioners. Hiring can favor curiosity and integrity, with technical skills taught later. Each crisis can be used to fix root causes such as segmentation and patching instead of repeating the same fire drills. Recognition can reward collaboration and community work rather than long hours, and teams with varied backgrounds and thinking are easier to defend. Bystander intervention and clear codes of conduct are also offered as ways to challenge toxic behaviour.

talks.title: Medical Devices - Security and Privacy Issues
talks.teaser: Explores how implanted and wearable medical devices expose personal health data and the security flaws behind it.
talks.summary:
The session opens with the case for medical devices, from pacemakers and insulin pumps to retinal implants and fitness trackers, and explains why patients accept them despite their risks. The speakers argue that these devices collect intimate data, and that people generally want that data kept private even when they share it casually.

The middle of the talk covers privacy and security. They describe how device transmissions carry identifiers such as names, dates of birth and serial numbers, and cite a 2013 study in which a few coarse data points singled out most people in a large dataset. They point to recurring flaws across devices, a 2022 figure that most medical IoT devices have known security gaps, and historical NSA slides on collecting medical "pattern of life" data. Basic hardware is outlined as well: a microcontroller, sensors, ISM-band radios and near-field communication.

The speakers then present their own devices. Pam describes her spinal stimulator and its near-field programmer, which has no login, and adjusts it live on stage. Jim, who joined remotely, is covered through a recorded demonstration of his defibrillator and a Q&A. The talk closes by noting that vendor support, device lifetimes and the limits of RF shielding pouches leave patients with few practical options.

talks.title: PEnnsylvania 6-5000: A Hacker Farewell to the Hotel Pennsylvania
talks.teaser: Traces the history of the Hotel Pennsylvania and the hacker conference memories made in its halls and basements.
talks.summary:
This closing-night retrospective looks back at the Hotel Pennsylvania, the Midtown New York building that hosted a hacker conference for many years before its demolition. The speakers open with the building's history, covering its 1919 opening, its many name changes, its ties to Penn Station and its long, partly sealed basements, and they explain how the hotel's odd layout and dated fixtures shaped the event.

The middle of the session shifts to memories from staff and attendees. Stories cover the information desk and its improvised answers, the radio booth that broadcast the event to remote listeners, the badge designs from each year, a project that tried to map attendee interests with RFID, and a rooftop access problem that repeatedly drew security. Several tales are lighter, involving pranks, sleep in the hammock area and a makeshift shower service, while others touch on conduct issues the community had to handle.

The session closes by opening the floor to listeners in the room and online, who shared their own first-conference experiences. The takeaway is less about the building itself than about how an imperfect shared venue became a community space, and about the effort to preserve its history ahead of the move to a new location.

talks.title: Hack Cancer: How Hackers Can Help Save 9.5 Million Lives Every Year
talks.teaser: Traces a patient's cancer journey and proposes open, affordable approaches that could bring effective treatment to more people.
talks.summary:
Karamoon opens with a personal account: a terminal bowel cancer diagnosis in 2016 with a prognosis of seven to nine months. Rather than accept the limited options available in the UK, the speaker pursued treatment in Japan, combining surgery, several chemotherapy types, targeted drugs, radiation, hyperthermia and immunotherapy over four years, followed by a year of low-dose maintenance chemotherapy.

The middle of the talk explains why cancer is hard to treat. It is a family of diseases tied to abnormal cell division and failed cell death, it can spread from where it started, and it often produces no symptoms until late. Treatments themselves suppress the immune system, which the speaker argues is central to long-term survival. Across survivors, four patterns seemed to matter: the condition of the immune system, access to the newest treatments, the total treatment load, and the variety of approaches, which makes it harder for tumours to evolve resistance.

The closing section sketches a blueprint. Existing effective treatments could be re-engineered to cut the cost and size of equipment such as scanners and radiotherapy machines, and drugs whose patents have expired could be turned into lower-cost versions through non-profit or open-source efforts. The speaker also called for better knowledge sharing among patients, doctors and researchers, and stressed that the talk is not medical advice.

talks.title: Biological Time Hacking
talks.teaser: Explains how light, sleep cycles and focus rhythms can be adjusted to free up more usable waking hours.
talks.summary:
The speaker argues that time is worth more than money, because lost hours cannot be recovered, and that biological needs such as breathing, eating, sleeping and concentrating set the daily schedule more firmly than personal intentions do. Small repeated delays, like waiting for coffee, and interruptions that force a mind to re-focus add up over a year. The stated aim is to reclaim usable hours, not to pursue general health.

Much of the talk centres on light and rhythm. The eye contains cells that sense light and tell the brain what time of day it is, so bright blue light in the morning supports alertness, while dim red light at night is far less disruptive to sleep. Sleep runs in roughly 90-minute cycles, which makes a short nap timed around a coffee's delayed effect a practical option. Focus, too, seems to fade after about 90 minutes, so long tasks benefit from breaks. Other tactics include light before waking and drinking fluids during sleep, while eating during sleep proved harder.

In questions, the speaker acknowledged that sensitivity to light and caffeine varies widely between people, and that polyphasic sleep, tried earlier, was dropped because it was socially inconvenient. The closing advice is to treat these methods as personal experiments, match demanding work to peak energy periods, and plan the day around the body's own schedule.

talks.title: Cast-Away: A DIY Platform for Video Capture, Automation, and Various Antics
talks.teaser: Shows a low-cost Raspberry Pi setup for capturing, monitoring and analyzing analog and broadcast TV with computer vision.
talks.summary:
Adam Tannir presents Cast-Away, a hobbyist platform for recording and analyzing television, both from old VHS tapes and from live broadcast signals. He explains the motivation: vintage tapes hold unusual shows and commercials, and once cable providers encrypted over-the-air channels, he turned to an antenna and a digital tuner box instead.

The hardware section covers inexpensive USB capture dongles for digital and analog video, VLC settings that favor low latency and MJPEG output, and a Raspberry Pi 4 that needs a heatsink and fan. The board's infrared receiver can be enabled through the kernel to act as a remote control, and the same setup doubles as a compact keyboard-video-mouse solution for a second machine. For analysis, OpenCV and imutils handle frames from live or recorded sources, and a background-averaging filter highlights motion while isolating static scenes. Ideas include commercial detection, barcode-style visualizations of episodes, pose estimation for fight scenes, and automated caption capture.

The talk closes with archival examples, including a recording from about 1983 featuring stations that no longer exist and a rerun carrying an ad for NeXTSTEP. Tannir notes that the code is still small, starting from a Flask streaming example, and presents the project as a work in progress that others can extend.

talks.title: Hackers Can Help: Open Technical Problems in Investigative Journalism
talks.teaser: Lays out unsolved technical problems in data journalism, from web scraping and PDF extraction to OCR and form parsing.
talks.summary:
Brandon Roberts, a self-taught data journalist who works with newsrooms, opens by arguing that many technical projects aimed at news miss the mark. He points to bias detectors and troll-hunting tools that tend to be vague or unreliable, while records-request tooling, a practical need for reporters, is scarcely present in public code repositories.

He then walks through the usual data journalism pipeline: gathering material through scraping or public records requests, pulling structured information out of PDFs and scanned pages, and assembling datasets. Each stage has gaps. Scrapers on government sites break on JavaScript, pop-up alerts and slow page loads; PDF extraction tools work only on clean layouts; OCR struggles with large leaks such as the Panama Papers archive and with handwritten complaint logs; and campaign finance forms vary from outlet to outlet, so no single template fits. He notes that much existing machine learning serves commercial problems rather than these.

He closes by urging technical people to build shareable tools and datasets, and to partner with local newsrooms and academics, while being transparent about bias and mindful of budgets and exclusivity terms. He lists groups such as NICAR, OpenNews and Big Local News as entry points for getting involved.

talks.title: School Districts Should Not Be in the Business of Intelligence Collection
talks.teaser: Examines a Fairfax County school district's plan to buy social media intelligence tooling and the oversight gaps it raises.
talks.summary:
Harry Jackson, a former intelligence officer and parent advocate, examines a request for proposal from Fairfax County Public Schools in Virginia. The solicitation sought software to widen a social media research program with the stated aim of catching threats, and Jackson argues it reads more like an open-ended intelligence collection effort than a safety tool.

He walks through the document against the standard intelligence cycle, from planning and collection through processing, analysis and dissemination. In his reading, a vendor could treat brands, reputations and individual parents as targets, gather data beyond what people share voluntarily, scrape deep and dark web sources, and connect results to student records. He contrasts this with the legal thresholds that govern real intelligence agencies, says the sources would not be vetted to analytic standards, and warns that the output could be used to assemble targeting packages against critics of the board. He also ties the proposal to earlier disputes over public comment limits and the handling of parents who spoke out.

He closes with practical steps for parents and community members: file public records requests about district contracts, attend and monitor board meetings, and press for retention limits, encryption and clear oversight before any such system is bought. The main message is that procurement documents deserve as much scrutiny as the technology they describe.

talks.title: Hacking Comprehension: Overcoming Limitations to Better Understand the World
talks.teaser: Explores how perception and cognitive bias drive disagreement, and how mapping competing viewpoints might help people understand each other.
talks.summary:
Jamie Joyce, executive director of the Society Library, opens with a set of visual illusions, including the dress that split viewers into black-and-blue and gold-and-white camps and a pair of crocs that divided the room. The point is that prior experience shapes what the brain fills in from ambiguous input, so people looking at identical images can reach different conclusions, and even agree on something that is not actually present.

Midway through, the talk moves from perception to politics. Joyce argues that cognitive biases, limited attention, uneven access to expertise and different information diets make it hard for people to share a common picture of contested issues. She describes how the Society Library extracts claims, arguments and evidence from many kinds of sources and organizes them into a structured map, using a California nuclear plant as the worked example. Instead of a binary open-or-closed choice, the map surfaces around nine positions, each with the conditions under which people would accept it. Labeling weak or unsupported claims, and offering alternate reading levels, are presented as ways to aid comprehension.

The closing section raises unresolved questions about the ethics of inducing comprehension: how vivid or emotional presentation can persuade, who decides what gets amplified, and where framing becomes coercion. For practitioners building knowledge tools, the takeaway is that design choices carry bias risk and need explicit safeguards.

talks.title: Writing for the Ear
talks.teaser: Covers audiobook production, from choosing a book and planning recording gear to editing, delivery formats and narration.
talks.summary:
The talk starts by separating what counts as in scope: talking books built for navigation and access, audiobooks that offer a spoken text alongside or instead of print, and recitals, dramatizations and podcasts at the edges. The speaker, who produces talking books for a national library service, then advises on choosing material, steering away from religious texts, children's books, fan fiction and fast-changing technical books.

The middle covers gear, software and people. The speaker discourages all-in-one field recorders, Bluetooth headsets and open or in-ear monitoring, favoring a proper microphone with an XLR interface, closed headphones and a treated room, with Audacity as the main free editor. Production uses a narrator, an engineer who handles levels and storage, and a director who tracks performance and continuity. Quality control should come from a separate listener who flags errors quickly. Post-production advice covers lossless FLAC archives instead of MP3, bundling full project folders, and budgeting several hours of staff time per finished hour.

Narration tips include reading the book beforehand, leaving pauses between sentences, avoiding compression and text-to-speech, and recording room tone at the start. The speaker notes that home-recorded projects often need heavier repair later. The Q&A covered author-read versus cold readings, and the talk closes with a call for more human narrators.

talks.title: Can You Travel Without Physically Moving? "Online Lodging" to "Virtual Travel"
talks.teaser: Shows how a COVID-19 antigen test kit was repurposed into a foldable headset for virtual travel experiences.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with the pandemic ending most intercontinental travel. A friend working for a small Japanese municipality hit by the 2011 tsunami asked the speaker, an artist and researcher based in the Netherlands, how to spend leftover budget from a cancelled culinary residency. The speaker drew on "online lodging," a format in which guesthouses in Japan ran video calls that recreated the conversations of a shared common room, and on the idea of a region split into two overlapping places, as in a city-state novel. The project paired a Dutch coastal city with the Japanese town as two halves of one virtual region.

The middle of the talk covers the work itself. Artists were commissioned to film local places on phones, to make 360-degree videos, paintings and face-in-scene photo experiences. The centerpiece reused the box design of a home antigen test kit. The package contained a foldable headset that looked nearly identical to a test kit and resembled a cardboard viewer. Buyers assemble it, insert a phone and launch an app, skipping the testing and travel-permit steps. Demonstrations covered iOS and Android apps with scenes such as a sauna, a seaside view and a pig farm.

In the Q&A, the speaker said the project came from specific circumstances and that turning it into a series would not be of interest. The main takeaway is the framing of travel as something shaped by a local person's perspective, and of pandemic gaps as a space for new design.
